title_en: Why a $2 Billion Law Firm Suddenly Collapsed
title_zh: 一家 $20 亿律所为何突然崩塌：对话 Yale Law School 教授 John Morley
subtitle_zh: 从 Weil Gotshal 倒闭剖析律所合伙制的“挤兑”逻辑、造雨人与代际冲突。
description: Why a $2 Billion Law Firm Suddenly Collapsed

turns.en: So while Gottschall collapsed, there's some irony here because it's. perhaps most famous for being a bankruptcy firm. It worked on stuff like the General Motors bankruptcy, Lehman Brothers as well, I think. And now itself has failed. And of course, this has prompted a lot of questions about the durability of the big law model. And I'm going to give my standard caveat whenever we do a legal episode, which is my husband was a lawyer. Neither of us enjoyed it very much. But one thing I learned from that entire experience is the law model is just so weird.
turns.zh: Weil Gotshal 倒闭了，这里面有点讽刺，因为它或许最出名的身份，恰恰是一家破产律所。它做过 General Motors 的破产案，我想还有 Lehman Brothers。结果现在它自己倒下了。这当然引发了很多关于大所模式（big law model）能否持久的疑问。每次做法律相关的选题，我都会给出我那句标准的免责声明：我丈夫以前是律师，我们俩都不太享受那段经历。但我从这整段经历里学到的一点是，律所这种模式实在是太奇怪了。

turns.en: It's weird.
turns.zh: 是很奇怪。

turns.en: And no one seems to be particularly happy with it. Like, neither the partners.
turns.zh: 而且似乎没有人对它特别满意。比如说，合伙人们也不满意。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Partners probably more so than some other people, but certainly not, like, junior associates. And law firms, they're always going through these efforts where they try to, like, fix things. You know, they start de-equitizing some of the partners or try to move out some of the older partners, try to make life better for some of the junior associates. And they never seem to quite get it right.
turns.zh: 合伙人可能比其他人更甚，但初级律师（junior associates）肯定也不满意。律所总是在做各种努力，想去把问题解决掉。你知道，他们会把一部分合伙人“去股权化”（de-equitizing），或者把一些年长的合伙人请走，试着让初级律师的日子好过一点。可他们似乎总也做不到位。

turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 是没有。

turns.en: And this seems totally true. I do not know much either about law firms, how they're structured from a corporate perspective, and also law firms, how they're structured from a corporate perspective in theory, as in what is the theory such that Maybe people don't like this system, but it seems to be the least worst system. It does not seem easily changeable. I know that law firms are basically like, they're never public. They never have like outside equity holders and so forth. There are some publicly traded law firms.
turns.zh: 这话听起来完全没错。我对律所也不怎么了解——无论是它们从公司角度实际上是怎么搭起来的，还是理论上应该怎么搭，就是说，背后的理论究竟是什么，以至于也许大家都不喜欢这套体系，但它似乎又是所有选项里最不坏的一个，而且看起来很难改。我知道律所基本上从不上市，从不会有外部股权持有人之类的。不过也有一些上市交易的律所。

turns.en: I don't know if they're publicly traded, but they have outside investors. But you're right. You do know one thing about law firms, which is the standard model is the partnership model, right?
turns.zh: 我不确定它们是不是真上市了，但它们确实有外部投资人。不过你说得对，你确实了解律所的一件事：标准模式就是合伙制（partnership model），对吧？

turns.en: Yeah, standard partnership is the partnership model. And you know what's funny is like, okay, we had this collapse of a pretty big law firm. Didn't seem to be a big deal in the sense like, Unlike, say, if there was an equivalent bank that had collapsed, you'd be like, oh, panic. What does it mean? Seems like it just sort of happened and life went on. But the other interesting thing, too, is I remember in 2008 when a lot of the banks literally did collapse. And people were like, oh, this wouldn't have happened if they hadn't abandoned the partnership model and stuff like that. But I guess partnerships aren't immune to collapse either.
turns.zh: 对，标准的合伙制就是合伙模式。有意思的是，好，我们看到一家挺大的律所倒了，可这事好像也没什么大不了的——不像要是一家同体量的银行倒了，你会想“哦，恐慌了，这意味着什么？”。律所倒闭好像就这么发生了，日子照过。但另一件有意思的事是，我记得 2008 年很多银行真的倒了的时候，大家会说“哦，要不是它们放弃了合伙制，这事就不会发生”之类的。可我想，合伙制也一样免不了倒闭。

turns.en: Well, this is exactly what I was going to say because I've been thinking about the partnership model because both of us read Lloyd Blankfein's biography earlier this year. And you can tell he is very wistful for the old partnership model that they had at Goldman Sachs until they IPO'd.
turns.zh: 嗯，这正是我要说的，因为我一直在琢磨合伙制这个事——我们俩今年早些时候都读了 Lloyd Blankfein 的传记。你能看出来，他对 Goldman Sachs 上市（IPO）之前的老合伙制非常怀念。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: We should talk about how law firms ended up being partnerships, why they collapsed. Why does it seem like rainmakers are such a huge thing in the legal industry such that they can basically lead to the collapse of a single firm like basically overnight? And this does have broader importance beyond just the legal industry when you think about ownership problems. of firms, there is this like fundamental question of whether or not it's better for a firm to be owned by its workers directly or by outside investors.
turns.zh: 我们该聊聊律所最后怎么变成了合伙制、它们又为什么会倒闭。为什么在律师行业里，“造雨人”（rainmakers，指能带来大客户大业务的合伙人）似乎是这么重要的一件事，以至于他们基本上能让一整家律所几乎一夜之间就倒掉？而且当你想到公司的所有权问题时，这确实有超出律师行业本身的更广泛意义——这里有一个根本性的问题：一家公司究竟是由它的员工直接持有更好，还是由外部投资人持有更好。

turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全同意。

turns.en: You know, like we go down every year, we go down to the future proof conference and there's a bunch of registered investment advisor, independent investment advisors, et cetera. And, you know, you always hear, I'm always interested in hearing how they, those small financial advisors structure their thing. And often there's like a founder or, And then they like sell their equity over time when they're ready to retire to the junior. People come up and maybe take out loans. I'm very interested in these different corporate structures and how they how people make them work and evidently how sometimes they don't work.
turns.zh: 你知道，我们每年都会去 future proof 那个会议，那儿有一堆注册投资顾问（registered investment advisor）、独立投资顾问等等。我总是很有兴趣听他们讲，那些小型财务顾问是怎么搭自己的架构的。通常会有个创始人，然后等他们准备退休的时候，就慢慢把股权卖给下面的年轻人，年轻人可能还会去贷款来接手。我对这些不同的公司架构、人们怎么让它运转起来、以及显然有时候它们怎么运转不起来，都非常感兴趣。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: And how they don't work. Okay, so we do, in fact, have the perfect guest. We're going to be speaking with John Morley. He is a professor at Yale Law School. More importantly, perhaps, he published an academic paper that was very prescient in predicting, I guess, some of the pressures that can come to bear on a law firm through the partnership model. So, Professor Morley, thanks so much for coming on All Thoughts.
turns.zh: 以及它们怎么运转不起来。好，那我们确实请到了最合适的嘉宾。我们今天要和 John Morley 对谈。他是 Yale Law School 的教授。或许更重要的是，他发表过一篇很有先见之明的学术论文，我认为它相当精准地预言了合伙制可能给一家律所带来的一些压力。那么，Morley 教授，非常感谢您来做客 Odd Lots。

turns.en: Thanks for inviting me. It's a pleasure to be here.
turns.zh: 谢谢你们邀请我，很荣幸来到这里。

turns.en: Why don't I start with a very basic question, but how did we end up in... a world where the vast majority of big law firms are partnerships. So I mentioned there are some exceptions, famous exceptions, particularly in the UK, but the vast majority of them are owned by the actual partners. How did this come to be a thing?
turns.zh: 那我先从一个很基础的问题开始：我们是怎么走到……这么一个世界的——绝大多数大所都是合伙制。我前面提到有一些例外，一些著名的例外，尤其是在英国，但绝大多数律所都是由真正的合伙人自己持有的。这是怎么成为主流的？

turns.en: It's not entirely clear, surprisingly. There's not an obvious answer to that question. I'll answer the question, though, on three levels. So the first is history. Law firms started out this way. And because it doesn't require a lot of capital to start a law firm, it really just requires the labor of the workers and the human capital of the workers, you can start one without having outside investors. And so large law firms didn't appear, and by large I mean even more than three or four lawyers, didn't appear until the mid-19th century in either the United States or the United Kingdom, but they've always been worker-owned. The second level in which I'll answer that question is regulation. Today... The model rules of professional conduct, which have been adopted in some form in almost every state, generally require that a law firm be owned by lawyers, which as a practical matter tends to mean the lawyers who work at the firm. Then there's a third level at which we could answer that question, which is economics. Big, big debate about whether this pattern of ownership is efficient or not. Should law firms instead be owned by their investors? The best answer to that question was given by a Yale Law School professor named Henry Hansman, who was my teacher and mentor. His argument was that in a law firm, the contributions of the workers are relatively easy to measure and perceive, which reduces the risk of conflict among the workers. Imagine if General Motors were owned by its workers, there would be huge conflict between the management and the people on the factory floor. There'd be lots of conflict about how much each of the executives pay because it'll be hard to measure their relative contributions. In a law firm, it's much easier to measure people's contributions because they bill by the hour. And you can often identify which clients they brought in.
turns.zh: 说来出人意料，这事并不完全清楚。这个问题没有一个显而易见的答案。不过我会从三个层面来回答。第一个是历史。律所一开始就是这个样子。因为开一家律所并不需要很多资本，它真正需要的是员工的劳动力和人力资本（human capital），所以你在没有外部投资人的情况下也能开一家。因此大型律所——我说的大型，哪怕只是三四个律师以上——直到 19 世纪中叶才在美国或英国出现，但它们一直都是员工持有的。我回答这个问题的第二个层面是监管。今天……《职业行为示范规则》（Model Rules of Professional Conduct）几乎在每个州都以某种形式被采纳，它通常要求律所必须由律师持有，而在实际操作中，这往往就意味着由在这家所里执业的律师持有。还有第三个层面可以回答这个问题，那就是经济学。关于这种所有权模式是否高效，有一场非常大的辩论：律所是否应该改由投资人持有？这个问题最好的答案，来自一位名叫 Henry Hansmann 的 Yale Law School 教授，他是我的老师和导师。他的论点是：在一家律所里，员工的贡献相对容易衡量和感知，这就降低了员工之间发生冲突的风险。想象一下如果 General Motors 由它的员工持有，管理层和车间工人之间就会有巨大的冲突；关于每个高管该拿多少报酬也会有很多争执，因为很难衡量他们的相对贡献。而在律所里，衡量一个人的贡献要容易得多，因为他们是按小时计费的（bill by the hour），而且你往往能认出哪些客户是他带进来的。

turns.en: This is the eat what you kill model, right?
turns.zh: 这就是所谓“自己打猎自己吃”（eat what you kill）的模式，对吧？

turns.en: That's right. That's the eat what you kill model. But even before the eat what you kill model, there were even simpler ways of identifying lawyers' productivity and structuring their pay, which was that every lawyer of a given level of seniority got paid the same amount. So worker ownership is more tenable in a law firm than in other kinds of businesses because the workers tend to be more similar to one another. That's the idea.
turns.zh: 没错，那就是 eat what you kill 模式。但甚至在 eat what you kill 模式之前，还有更简单的办法来识别律师的产出、并设计他们的薪酬，那就是同一资历级别的每个律师拿一样的报酬。所以在律所里，员工持有比在其他类型的企业里更站得住脚，因为员工之间往往彼此更相似。这就是那个思路。

turns.en: So let's say I'm a private equity guy and I look at a law firm, maybe a medium-scale law firm. And I look at it and I say, I bet they could do service just as well to their clients as they do just as well if they got rid of all their junior partners and replaced them with this AI solution that I developed. So I'm going to invest in them millions of dollars, tell them to stop hiring new juniors and use AI instead. Why doesn't that happen? Is there a legal thing? Why can't, let's talk about like, someone must have, people have this idea. People look at law firms and see opportunities for productivity gains. Are there legal reasons that this cannot be done?
turns.zh: 那假设我是个私募股权（private equity）的人，我看上一家律所，也许是一家中等规模的律所。我看着它心想：我敢打赌，就算把他们所有的初级合伙人都裁掉、换成我开发的这套 AI 方案，他们一样能服务好客户。所以我要投给他们几百万美元，让他们别再招新的初级律师，改用 AI。为什么这种事不会发生？是有法律上的障碍吗？我们来聊聊——总得有人想过这个，人们看着律所、看到了提升生产力的机会。是有法律上的原因导致这事做不成吗？

turns.en: So first off, there are investor-backed, venture-backed businesses doing that now. Okay. It's harder to do that with a traditional law firm. In both types of businesses, the venture-backed businesses and traditional law firms, you have these rules that prohibit non-lawyer ownership. The way the venture-backed businesses get around those rules is by segregating the business into two chunks that each go into a different entity with a slightly different set of owners. On the one hand, you have the law firm, which provides legal services and employs lawyers and is owned exclusively by the lawyers. On the other hand, you have what's called a managed service organization or MSO. The MSO is owned by a mix of investors and the lawyers who work at the law firm. And the MSO does everything other than provide legal advice. Oh. It employs the word processing people, the administrative assistants, the finance, the accountants, the financial administrators. It holds the lease. It owns the computers. Oh, I see. And so basically what happens is the clients pay fees to the law firm, and then the law firm pays a price for administrative support to the MSO.
turns.zh: 首先，现在确实有投资人支持、风投支持的企业在这么干。好。对一家传统律所来说，这么干更难。在这两类企业里——风投支持的企业和传统律所——你都会碰到这些禁止非律师持有（non-lawyer ownership）的规则。风投支持的企业绕过这些规则的办法，是把业务拆成两块，各自装进一个不同的实体，两个实体的所有者结构略有不同。一方面，你有律所，它提供法律服务、雇佣律师，并且完全由律师持有。另一方面，你有一个所谓的管理服务组织（managed service organization，简称 MSO）。MSO 由投资人和在律所工作的律师混合持有。MSO 负责除了提供法律建议之外的一切。哦。它雇佣文字处理人员、行政助理、财务、会计、财务管理人员。它持有租约。它拥有电脑。哦，我明白了。所以基本上发生的情况是：客户把费用付给律所，然后律所再为行政支持向 MSO 付一笔钱。

turns.en: So this makes a lot of sense. Just real quickly, when you say there are these rules about ownership from non-lawyers, are these state laws? Are they— Where do these rules come from?
turns.zh: 这很讲得通。我就快速问一下，你说有这些关于非律师持有的规则，这些是州法律吗？它们是——这些规则是从哪儿来的？

turns.en: Yeah, they're essentially legal ethics rules adopted by state bar associations and sometimes by state legislatures. The American Bar Association has promulgated a model set of rules called the Model Rules of Professional Conduct. And every state has adopted them in some form. A couple of states, namely Arizona and Utah, have altered those model rules to permit non-lawyer ownership of law firms, but only those states. Okay.
turns.zh: 对，它们本质上是各州律师协会（state bar associations）、有时是州议会制定的法律职业道德规则。美国律师协会（American Bar Association）颁布了一套示范规则，叫《职业行为示范规则》（Model Rules of Professional Conduct）。每个州都以某种形式采纳了它。有两个州，也就是 Arizona 和 Utah，修改了这套示范规则，允许非律师持有律所，但只有这几个州。好。

turns.en: So the working narrative of what went wrong at Weill Gottschall is this idea of all the rainmakers departed. A bunch of senior partners who had really strong client relationships started walking away from the firm, and then it snowballed from there. And we'll get into the snowballing because this is basically the essence of a lot of your academic research on this topic. But just on the Rainmaker model itself, this is something that I have never understood about law firms because you think about the law firm as an organization that they should want clients to be sticky and loyal to the firm itself. But then in practice, the relationships that are sticky are between an individual lawyer and an individual client. So when a partner walks away, they walk away with, I don't know, like $ 300 million worth of business from a specific client. Why is that a thing? Why haven't law firms done more to, I guess, institutionalize some of these relationships?
turns.zh: 那么，关于 Weil Gotshal 出了什么问题，通行的说法是这样：所有的“造雨人”都走了。一批客户关系非常硬的资深合伙人开始离开这家所，然后就从那儿开始滚雪球。我们待会儿会聊到这个滚雪球，因为这基本上就是你在这个课题上很多学术研究的核心。但就先说造雨人这个模式本身，这是我对律所一直想不通的一点：你会觉得律所作为一个组织，应该希望客户是粘住这家所、忠于这家所本身的。可现实里，真正粘的关系是发生在某一个律师和某一个客户之间的。所以当一个合伙人走人的时候，他会带着——我不知道——比如某个特定客户价值 3 亿美元的业务一起走。为什么会这样？律所为什么没有做更多，去把这些关系“机构化”（institutionalize）一些呢？

turns.en: Because it's hard. is the answer. There's always a tension between law firm management on the one hand and individual partners on the other. The management wants to institutionalize all the clients and make sure that the client's loyalty is to the firm, not the partner. The partner wants to keep the clients individual to the partner so that the partner can leave. And also because under an eat what you kill system, the partner might get credit for bringing the business in, which means that the partner wants to make sure that the across other partners as well. And there's a way in which law firms are undermining their own objectives by adopting a what you kill system. If you pay partners for tethering their clients' loyalty personally to themselves, that is naturally what they will do. But on the other hand, if you don't pay them for doing that, well, then they'll sit back and wait for other people to generate business. It's what in economics we call an optimization problem. You're trading off two variables that are in tension with one another.
turns.zh: 答案就是：因为难。律所管理层和个体合伙人之间始终存在一种张力。管理层想把所有客户都机构化，确保客户的忠诚是对着这家所、而不是对着某个合伙人。而合伙人则想把客户绑在自己个人身上，这样他随时能走人。而且在 eat what you kill 体系下，合伙人还可能因为带进业务而拿到分成，这意味着合伙人也想确保这一点——对其他合伙人来说也一样。有一种情况是，律所采用 eat what you kill 体系，反而在破坏它自己的目标。如果你付钱给合伙人、奖励他们把客户的忠诚个人化地绑在自己身上，那他们自然会这么做。可反过来，如果你不为这件事付钱给他们，那他们就会往那儿一坐，等着别人去创收。这在经济学里我们叫它一个优化问题（optimization problem）。你是在两个彼此冲突的变量之间做权衡。

turns.en: We'll get back to the, maybe the original sin. It sounds like the original sin for a while, maybe it goes back to 2013 or something. But if we're in the sort of like the final few months of the firm this year, a big rainmaker walks out the door. I'm still in the door. Tell me why that's bad for me. Because we're describing, all right, there's this bank run like pressure, or I think you call it a partner run, but whatever. It's a bank run like pressure. What bad happens for the remaining partners when a rainmaker walks out the door?
turns.zh: 我们待会儿会回到那个，也许是最初的原罪（original sin）。听起来这个原罪已经有一阵子了，也许能追溯到 2013 年之类的。但如果我们把时间放到今年这家所最后的几个月：一个大造雨人走出了门，而我还待在门里。告诉我，为什么这对我是坏事？因为我们描述的是——好，有这么一种类似银行挤兑（bank run）的压力，或者我想你管它叫“合伙人挤兑”（partner run），反正差不多。它是一种类似银行挤兑的压力。当一个造雨人走出门的时候，留下来的合伙人会遭遇什么坏事？

turns.en: Okay, so let's break it into two pieces. One is how does that partner's departure damage the firm? Yeah. And second, how do the other partners get hurt as a result?
turns.zh: 好，我们把它拆成两部分。第一部分是，那个合伙人的离开是怎么损害这家所的？对。第二部分是，其他合伙人因此是怎么受伤的？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Okay, so the first piece is when that partner leaves, especially if that partner's a rainmaker and especially if that partner's clients are personally loyal to him or her, then that partner will take revenues with her, right? The clients will leave immediately. And the firm will have fewer revenues as a result. Now, that's not obviously bad for the firm because in addition to losing revenues, it also gets rid of some costs. You no longer have to pay that partner the partner's compensation. And indeed, sometimes law firms deliberately fire or de-equitize partners because the partners are bringing in less than they're taking out. But if the partner is bringing in more than they're taking out, then to lose the partner is a loss. Here's the bigger issue, though. You often can't cut costs as quickly as you lose revenues. So when the partner leaves, you still got to pay the lease on that partner's corner office. And you can lay off associates, but that's kind of a bad thing to do. You can lay off staff, but that's a bad thing to do. You might have debts to pensioners and retirees from the firm. You might have bank debts, none of which go away simply because that partner left. There might also be other partners who depend on that partner for work. If I'm an M & A partner, for example, I'm expected to bring in business. But if I'm a tax partner, all I really do is work on business brought in by the M & A partners. So if the M & A guy leaves, well, we still got to pay the tax partners and now they don't have any business. So you can't cut costs as quickly as you can cut revenues. The answer to the second piece is a bit more complicated. Why does that hurt the partners who stay? Well, the answer is because the partners are owners of the firm and not merely employees. And that causes them to suffer for two reasons. The first is that as owners of the firm, they are paid in shares of the profits. And so if the revenues have gone down while the costs have stayed fixed, the profits have to go down as well. That's just simple math, which means that once that rainmaker has left, there are fewer profits left over to pay the partners who remain. Just as a matter of arithmetic, they can't all be paid the same. So their pay has to go down. The second reason they suffer is that if the firm eventually files for bankruptcy, and we'll talk about the snowball or the run that might propel it into a bankruptcy, but if it ever does wind down, the partners can face a bunch of forms of liability that are unique to their status as owners of the firm. The most important is a doctrine called fraudulent transfer liability. The basic intuition behind that doctrine is that We don't want a debtor to give away assets on the eve of bankruptcy. If I'm about to file for bankruptcy, we don't want me to give away my car and my house to my girlfriend and my uncle. So basic rules of bankruptcy say if you give away money between the period you become insolvent and the period you file for bankruptcy, all of those giveaways can be voided or clawed back by the creditors. And here's the catch. A distribution on profits is a giveaway under that doctrine because it doesn't actually have to be paid. Wages have to be paid because they're contractual debts. If your administrative assistants have worked for two weeks, they've accrued a debt that they have a right to claim against the firm. By contrast, all the partners are entitled to receive is a discretionary distribution of dividends, which the firm can choose not to pay. So, for example, Berkshire Hathaway is sitting on billions of dollars of profits, which it's never paid out as a dividend because it doesn't have to. So what happens in law firm bankruptcies is after the firm goes south, the creditors show up and say, look, there was a 10-month period during which we consider the firm to have been insolvent, but during which you were making payments to partners. We want to claw that all back. And the partners say, you can't do that. We were workers. Those were wages. And the courts say, uh-uh. You were not employees. You were owners of the firm, and those weren't wages. Those were discretionary distributions of profits, which standard law can be clawed back in bankruptcy.
turns.zh: 好，第一部分是：当那个合伙人离开时，尤其如果他是造雨人、尤其如果他的客户是个人化地忠于他本人的，那么他会把营收一起带走，对吧？客户会立刻跟着走。结果这家所的营收就更少了。不过这未必对律所是坏事，因为在损失营收的同时，它也甩掉了一些成本。你不用再付那个合伙人的薪酬了。而且事实上，律所有时候会故意开除或者“去股权化”某些合伙人，因为这些人带进来的比他们拿走的少。但如果那个合伙人带进来的比他拿走的多，那么失去他就是一种损失。不过更大的问题在这儿：你削减成本的速度，往往赶不上你损失营收的速度。所以当合伙人走了，你还得付他那间转角办公室的租金。你可以裁掉初级律师，但这事儿挺难看的；你可以裁掉员工，但这也难看。你可能对这家所的退休金领取者、退休合伙人负有债务；你可能有银行债务——这些都不会仅仅因为那个合伙人走了就消失。还可能有别的合伙人要指望那个人给活干。比方说如果我是个并购（M&A）合伙人，大家期望我去带业务进来；但如果我是个税务合伙人，我真正做的就是处理并购合伙人带进来的业务。所以如果那个做并购的家伙走了，嗯，我们还是得付钱给税务合伙人，可现在他们没有任何业务了。所以你没法像砍营收那样快地砍成本。第二部分的回答要更复杂一些。为什么这会伤到留下来的合伙人？答案是：因为合伙人是这家所的所有者，而不仅仅是雇员。这让他们因为两个原因而受苦。第一，作为这家所的所有者，他们拿的是利润的份额。所以如果营收下降了、而成本保持固定，利润也就必然下降。这就是简单的算术，意味着一旦那个造雨人走了，剩下能分给留下来的合伙人的利润就更少了。纯粹从算术上讲，他们不可能都拿一样的钱，所以他们的报酬必须下降。他们受苦的第二个原因是：如果这家所最终申请破产——我们会聊到那个可能把它推向破产的滚雪球或者挤兑——但如果它真的要清盘，合伙人可能面临一系列因其所有者身份而独有的责任。最重要的是一种叫“欺诈性转让责任”（fraudulent transfer liability）的原则。这个原则背后的基本直觉是：我们不希望一个债务人在破产前夕把资产白送出去。如果我就快申请破产了，我们不希望我把我的车、我的房子送给我的女朋友和我叔叔。所以破产法的基本规则规定：如果你从资不抵债那一刻起、到申请破产这段时间里把钱送出去，所有这些赠与都可以被债权人撤销或者追回（clawed back）。而这里有个陷阱：在这个原则下，利润分配算是一种赠与，因为它其实并不是必须支付的。工资是必须付的，因为它们是合同债务。如果你的行政助理已经工作了两周，他们就积累了一笔有权向这家所主张的债务。相比之下，合伙人有权拿到的，只是一种可自由裁量的股息分配，公司可以选择不付。比如说，Berkshire Hathaway 坐拥几十亿美元的利润，却从没把它当股息发出去过，因为它不必发。所以在律所破产里发生的情况是：这家所出问题之后，债权人上门说：“看，有 10 个月的时间，我们认为这家所当时已经资不抵债，可在这段时间里你们一直在给合伙人付钱。我们要把这些全部追回来。”合伙人说：“你们不能这么干，我们是劳动者，那些是工资。”而法院说：“呃-呃。你们不是雇员。你们是这家所的所有者，那些不是工资，而是可自由裁量的利润分配，按照标准法律，在破产里是可以被追回的。”

turns.en: So the more a partner thinks that a firm might be heading for failure, the more risk there is that their compensation could be clawed back and that they could be liable for some parts of the business if it actually fails completely. But let's go like one step back and talk to us about what happens in a partner's mind when they see another high profile partner leave the firm. What are the sort of cost benefit calculations that they're doing in their heads to where they're thinking like, oh, this guy's getting a lot of money to go to a competitor. Maybe I should be thinking about doing the same thing. But on the other hand, maybe I really like my firm. Maybe I really enjoy working in the structured finance unit of Allen and Overear. I don't know what. What are the sort of thoughts going through their heads?
turns.zh: 所以说，一个合伙人越是觉得这家所可能正走向失败，他面临的风险就越大——他的薪酬可能被追回，而且如果它真的彻底垮掉，他可能还要为业务的某些部分承担责任。但我们往回退一步，跟我们讲讲：当一个合伙人看到另一个高知名度的合伙人离开这家所时，他心里在发生什么。他们脑子里在做怎样的成本收益盘算，以至于会想“哦，这家伙去竞争对手那儿能拿到一大笔钱，也许我也该考虑做同样的事”；但另一方面又想“也许我是真的很喜欢我这家所，也许我是真的很享受在 Allen & Overy 的结构化融资部门工作”，我不知道。他们脑子里到底在转些什么念头？

turns.en: So this is what I call the leave-stay decision. You might not wake up as a law firm partner on a Wednesday morning and think, should I stay or should I go? But implicitly, You face that decision every day. And so you're going to walk through three kinds of calculus. The first is to say, well, because that guy left and took revenues with him and the costs of the firm are going to stay the same, we in the aggregate, me and my other partners, have to be paid less as a result. So I'm going to get paid less. But the amount I can get paid by moving across the street to Cravath is going to stay the same. So whereas previously I was making 5 million a while and being offered 4 million in Cravath, if now I'm making 3.9 a while, suddenly I might begin to move. The second thing I'll ask myself is, well, what about my liabilities? And I'll be saying, hmm, if everybody follows the same logic I'm following, they might leave before me. And then one guy leaves and another guy leaves and all of a sudden we're in a run on the bank. And if the firm ultimately collapses, I'm going to have to give back all or a portion of the money I received from the firm between now and the date of collapse. So suppose that I'm a partner while Gottschall in this past September. And I think most of my compensation is going to be paid to me in January. This is a typical feature of law firm compensation. Partners get paid a little bit every month or every quarter, and then they get paid a big chunk, maybe 50% or more of their compensation in January after the books for the prior year have been saddled. And you say, okay, it's September. I think there's a 50% chance this firm is gone in February. If it is, every dollar of compensation I receive between now and February is going to get taken back from me. So if I'm expecting $ 2 million in compensation over that period, I have to apply a 50% discount. It's really only worth a million to me. So then if Gibson Dunn comes and offers me $ 1. 5 million, it looks on paper like a pay cut because Weil's offering me two. But in fact, it's a pay raise because the expected value of Compit Weil is $ 1 million. Whereas at Gibson, it's 1.5 and it's also less risky. The third calculus I'll be making is what about the viability of my practice? So most law firms now, including Weill, have eat what you kill compensation systems. You get paid according to your productivity. Well, if I'm a tax lawyer and I'm in the business of servicing M & A deals brought in by M & A lawyers, then if all the M & A lawyers have left, I'm not going to look even to my own firm's managing partners as if I'm very productive. In other words, my own practice might become unsustainable. So as each partner leaves, the predicament of the remaining partners gets worse and worse. in a spiraling cycle that becomes a kind of run on the bank. That was excellent.
turns.zh: 这就是我所谓的“走还是留”的决策（leave-stay decision）。作为一个律所合伙人，你周三早上醒来可能不会想“我该留还是该走？”但潜移默化地，你每天都在面对这个决策。所以你会走过三种盘算。第一种是这么想：因为那个家伙走了、把营收带走了，而这家所的成本会保持不变，所以我们大家加起来——我和我其他的合伙人——结果就得少拿钱，那我也就会少拿。但我如果搬到街对面的 Cravath 去，他们能付给我的钱是不变的。所以，原来我在这儿拿 500 万、Cravath 给我开 400 万；可现在如果我在这儿只能拿 390 万了，那我忽然就可能开始动心了。我会问自己的第二件事是：那我的责任呢？我会想：嗯，如果每个人都按我在按的这套逻辑行事，他们可能会比我先走。然后一个走了、又一个走了，忽然之间我们就陷入了一场银行挤兑。如果这家所最终垮掉，我就得把从现在到垮台那天之间、我从这家所收到的钱，全部或者一部分吐出来。假设今年 9 月我是 Weil Gotshal 的一个合伙人，我想我大部分的薪酬会在 1 月付给我。这是律所薪酬的一个典型特征：合伙人每个月或者每个季度拿一点点，然后在 1 月——上一年的账结算完之后——拿到一大块，也许占他们薪酬的 50% 甚至更多。你会想：好，现在是 9 月，我觉得这家所有 50% 的概率在 2 月就没了。如果真没了，那从现在到 2 月之间我收到的每一美元薪酬都会被追回。所以如果我预计这段时间能拿 200 万美元薪酬，我就得打个五折，它对我来说其实只值 100 万。那么如果这时 Gibson Dunn 来给我开 150 万美元，纸面上看这像是降薪，因为 Weil 给我开的是 200 万；可实际上这是加薪，因为在 Weil 的薪酬期望值是 100 万，而在 Gibson 是 150 万，而且风险还更小。我要做的第三种盘算是：我这摊业务的可持续性怎么样？现在大多数律所，包括 Weil，都采用 eat what you kill 的薪酬体系，你按自己的产出来拿钱。那么，如果我是一个税务律师，我的活儿就是服务并购律师带进来的并购交易，那如果所有并购律师都走了，那么即便在我自己这家所的管理合伙人眼里，我看起来也不会很有产出。换句话说，我自己的这摊业务可能变得难以为继。所以每走掉一个合伙人，留下来的合伙人的处境就越来越糟，形成一个螺旋式下坠的循环，变成一种银行挤兑。这段讲得太精彩了。

turns.en: And I love this idea of like, even though the lawyer doesn't think so, actually in reality, every day they do wake up in the morning and make a decision whether they're going to leave or stay or Hard not to be reminded of the great 1882 essay, What is a Nation, by the French philosopher Ernest Renan, where he called a nation a daily referendum. And even though we don't vote every single day implicitly as citizens of a nation, we all decide every single day whether we want to continue on together as a nation. All right, let's try to talk more about Weil and the original sin here and why certain rainmakers perceived opportunities elsewhere is there an equivalent term like Wall Street for the legal magic circle is there like big law yeah what's is there like a term that's sort of like a what's like a anyway whatever elsewhere in the legal field listeners to the odd lots podcast know that a lot of money was made over the last several years and things like private credit, private equity, et cetera, all kinds of deal making. And everything I read seems to point to some like fateful early decisions in like 2013 coming out of the great financial crisis where while sort of like they sort of missed the boat on that. Do you agree with that characterization?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个说法：尽管律师自己并不这么想，但实际上每天早上醒来，他们确实都在做一个决定——是走还是留。这很难不让人想起法国哲学家 Ernest Renan 那篇伟大的 1882 年文章《什么是民族》（What is a Nation），他把民族称为一场“每日公投”（daily referendum）。尽管我们并不是每一天都真的去投票，但作为一个国家的公民，我们其实每天都在潜移默化地决定：我们是否愿意作为一个国家继续一起走下去。好，那我们试着多聊聊 Weil、聊聊这里的原罪，以及为什么某些造雨人在别处看到了机会。法律界有没有一个相当于华尔街“魔法圈”（magic circle）的说法？有没有类似“big law”这样的词？有没有一个什么——呃，反正不管叫什么。在律师行业里——Odd Lots 播客的听众都知道，过去几年在私募信贷（private credit）、私募股权等等各类交易撮合上，赚了很多很多钱。而我读到的一切都指向 2013 年前后、金融危机之后那几个命运攸关的早期决定——Weil 有点像是错过了那班船。你同意这个说法吗？

turns.en: I do. And I want to be clear. I don't have any inside knowledge about what. No, sure. I'm just speaking based on what I've read in news reports.
turns.zh: 我同意。而且我想说清楚：我并没有什么内部消息，关于……不，当然。我只是基于我在新闻报道里读到的东西来讲。

turns.en: But in terms of the news reports in your framework.
turns.zh: 那就以新闻报道、用你的框架来看。

turns.en: Yeah. I think one of the things that people found especially striking and prescient about my framework, if I can be a little bit immodest for a moment, I specifically predicted that a firm could collapse even when it had no meaningful debts and even when its profits were not just large but increasing. A firm can collapse basically whenever its profits are increasing. not increasing as quickly as its peers. In other words, what I call its relative profitability is decreasing. And that was unambiguously true of Weil. Weil's position in the profits per partner ranking fell from nine in 2020 to, I think, 20 in 2025. And I think that the fall was even starker if we go back further in history. So why did Weil fall relative to its peers? And I want to be clear, its profits were still increasing year over year. just not as quickly as Kirkland analysis. So why did Weill's profitability falter relative to its peers? I think the answer basically is that it didn't expand and it didn't shrink. Law is big law. That's the term that we'll use. Big law is in the midst of this sorting that actually resembles the sorting we've seen in many other industries, where the middle is getting hollowed out. And you're seeing this gravitation towards either becoming humongous or becoming really small. And Weil was uncomfortably in the middle. And that was a deliberate choice. My understanding is that there was a very powerful rainmaker there named Mike Aiello, whose departure in September was kind of the final straw that really, to mix metaphors here, pushed things over the edge. Aiello, understandably, in my opinion, wanted to work at a place that wasn't gigantic. He thought, you know, He was a little bit wistful, like Lloyd Blankfein, about the kind of smaller familial feel of the old Weill Gottschall, which is why, by the way, the firm he left for was Cravath, which still has that feel. But the problem was that Weill wasn't keeping pace with its competitors. And clients increasingly want firms that can offer a very large platform with a high degree of specialization. And that's something you can do if you're like Kirkland and Ellison, you're really gigantic. It's much harder to do on a smaller platform. There's only a couple of law firms that manage to stay small in the corporate transactional space and do really well. Basically, it's Wachtell and Cravath. But even those firms have been struggling. They've made it work by doing only very, very premium work on super-duper high-end stuff like public company M & A. But even those firms are experiencing a bunch of poaching. They are under profound pressure, and Weill just was not strong enough to withstand that.
turns.zh: 对。我想，人们觉得我的框架特别有冲击力、特别有先见之明的一点是——容我暂时不那么谦虚一下——我具体预言过：一家律所即便没有任何有意义的债务、即便它的利润不仅很大而且还在增长，它也可能倒闭。一家律所基本上可以在利润增长的时候倒闭——只要它增长得没有同行快。换句话说，我所谓的它的“相对盈利能力”（relative profitability）在下降。而这一点在 Weil 身上毫无疑义地成立。Weil 在“每合伙人利润”（profits per partner）排名里的位置，从 2020 年的第 9 名，跌到了——我想是——2025 年的第 20 名。而且我觉得如果我们往历史更前面看，这个下跌还要更陡。那么 Weil 为什么相对同行下滑了？我想说清楚，它的利润其实还在逐年增长，只是没有 Kirkland 那么快。那 Weil 的盈利能力为什么相对同行掉队了？我觉得答案基本上是：它既没有扩张，也没有收缩。律所就是 big law，这是我们要用的说法。big law 正处在一场洗牌之中，这场洗牌其实很像我们在很多其他行业看到的那种——中间层正在被掏空。你会看到大家都在往两端聚拢：要么变得超级巨大，要么变得非常小。而 Weil 就尴尬地卡在中间。而这其实是一个刻意的选择。据我理解，那里有一位非常有权势的造雨人，叫 Mike Aiello，他 9 月的离开，某种程度上就是压垮骆驼的最后一根稻草——请原谅我在这里混用了比喻——真正把事情推过了临界点。我觉得 Aiello 想离开是情有可原的，他想在一个不那么庞大的地方工作。他有点——就像 Lloyd Blankfein 一样——怀念老 Weil Gotshal 那种更小、更有家庭感的氛围，这也正是为什么，顺便说一句，他转投的那家所是 Cravath，因为 Cravath 至今还保留着那种感觉。但问题是，Weil 没能跟上它的竞争对手。客户越来越想要那种能提供非常大平台、并且高度专业化的律所。这件事如果你是 Kirkland & Ellis 那样真的巨无霸，你做得到；在一个更小的平台上就难得多。在公司交易（corporate transactional）领域，只有那么几家律所能既保持小体量又做得非常好，基本上就是 Wachtell 和 Cravath。但即便是这几家也一直在挣扎。它们之所以能做起来，是因为只做非常非常高端的活儿，只做超级高端的东西，比如上市公司并购。可即便是这几家，现在也遭遇了大量挖角。它们承受着巨大的压力，而 Weil 就是不够强，扛不住。

turns.en: Yeah, we've seen a similar dynamic in banking as well, right, where clients want the treasury functions. They want corporate M & A and everything basically offered on a single platform online. A lot of people will be listening to this and thinking, well, if so much of the business depends on single individuals or personalities or rainmakers, why don't law firms have non-competes that prevent them from just automatically leaving the firm and taking all their clients with them? What's the answer to that question?
turns.zh: 对，我们在银行业也见过类似的动态，对吧——客户想要资金管理部（treasury）的功能，想要公司并购，基本上所有东西都能在一个平台上、在线一站搞定。很多人听到这里会想：既然这么多业务都取决于单个的人、个人魅力或者造雨人，那律所为什么不设竞业禁止条款（non-competes），阻止他们说走就走、把客户全带走呢？这个问题的答案是什么？

turns.en: The answer is rule 5.6 of the model rules of professional conduct, which prohibit a lawyer from signing any agreement that would restrict their right to practice. So that includes non-competes and similar kinds of agreements. Now, to be clear, other countries don't have these rules. In the United Kingdom, lawyers are free to sign non-compete agreements, and law firms generally require that they do. And my understanding is that they are frequently enforced. Those restrictions also don't appear in other industries. You can impose those kinds of restrictions in accounting, in engineering, in management consulting. I would say, by the way, Joe, so you'd asked earlier, what is preventing investors from owning law firms? Well, one answer and the most commonly given answer is the one that I gave a moment ago, which is the rules limiting investor ownership. But another and perhaps more important answer is these rules prohibiting non-competes. And the reason is this. If you're a private equity fund looking at investing in a law firm, you're going to pay all these partners a bunch of cash to buy out their equity interests. And then what are they going to do? They can leave the next day.
turns.zh: 答案是《职业行为示范规则》的第 5.6 条，它禁止律师签署任何会限制其执业权利（right to practice）的协议。这就包括了竞业禁止以及类似性质的协议。不过要说清楚，其他国家没有这些规则。在英国，律师是可以自由签竞业禁止协议的，而且律所一般都要求他们签；据我理解，这些协议经常是被强制执行的。这类限制在其他行业也不存在。你可以在会计、工程、管理咨询行业里施加这种限制。顺便说一句，Joe，你前面问过，是什么在阻止投资人持有律所？一个答案——也是最常被给出的答案——就是我刚才讲的那个，也就是限制投资人持有的规则。但另一个、也许更重要的答案，是这些禁止竞业条款的规则。原因是这样：如果你是一家想投资律所的私募股权基金，你会付给这些合伙人一大笔现金，把他们的股权权益买断。然后他们会怎么做？他们第二天就能走人。

turns.en: They're going to leave, yeah.
turns.zh: 他们就会走人，对。

turns.en: And you can't force them to sign an agreement committing not to leave. So the best solution you have is to give them equity in the MSO and require them to forfeit that if they leave, because that's not a restriction on the lawyer's right to practice. That's a forfeiture condition on an equity stake in an unrelated business, in like a distinct business. It works pretty well, but whether it works well enough is going to be one of the central questions. of the new private equity boom in law firms. Okay.
turns.zh: 而你没法强迫他们签一份承诺不走的协议。所以你能想到的最好办法，就是给他们 MSO 的股权，并要求他们一旦离开就没收这部分股权，因为这不构成对律师执业权利的限制。它是一项针对一家无关企业——一家独立企业——里股权的没收条件。这招挺好使，但它到底够不够好使，将会是律所里这波新的私募股权热潮的核心问题之一。好。

turns.en: While it didn't grow as fast, it wasn't aggressive enough, et cetera. Maybe it was a little bit too conservative going back a couple of decades. Couldn't that have been rational from the perspective of senior lawyers? at the time, some of these decisions, maybe some of whom have retired by now. So it's like, we go back to like 2010. They're like, you know what? We don't need to like go super crazy on the private equity, private credit deal-making stuff. We think, and you know what? We're going to like trim some of our ranks and so forth. And maybe that set the seeds for their destruction in 2026. But if I'm maybe they retired in 2021, that seems like a big, especially now, again, like thinking about future investment or AI, et cetera, this sort of like intertemporal relationship of the lawyers and how long they're going to actually stay there and how much they care about what the firm is going to look like in 20 years.
turns.zh: 因为 Weil 增长得没那么快、不够激进等等，也许往前推几十年它有点太保守了。从当时那些资深律师的角度看，这些决定会不会其实是理性的？他们当中有些人现在也许已经退休了。就是说，我们回到 2010 年前后，他们心想：“你知道吗？我们不需要在私募股权、私募信贷那些交易撮合上搞得特别疯狂。”而且“你知道吗？我们要精简一下我们的队伍”之类的。也许这就为它们 2026 年的毁灭埋下了种子。但如果我是——也许他们 2021 年就退休了——那看起来就是一笔很大的……尤其现在，再想想未来的投资、AI 等等，这牵涉到律师的跨期（intertemporal）关系：他们究竟会在这儿待多久，以及他们有多在乎这家所 20 年后会长成什么样。

turns.en: Yeah, so look, it's hard to know the future. Law firms face the same uncertainty in business decision making that every other kind of business does. And let me say, there's lots of firms that took the path that Weill took, but most of them have since changed course. A good example is Cadwallader. The full name of Cadwallader was Cadwallader, Wickersham, and Taft. Haft being the former president and chief justice of the United States. It was a very, very prestigious, and Yale law professor, I might add. Very, very prestigious firm that was for a time extremely profitable. But like Weil, it didn't grow. And it eventually, very recently, had to find refuge in a merger with a much less prestigious firm. Hogan loves that. Apologies to all the people at Cadwallader and Hogan. But Hogan doesn't have the history that Cadwallader had. And so the point is to say Weil was not crazy. in pursuing the strategy. However, it was crazy and hanging onto it for a little too long. But you asked a deeper question, Joe, also, which was, are the partners of the present or past willing to invest for the future? Yeah. And the answer is, well, not necessarily. So I'm working on a new project that I recently put online about a concept that I call generational conflict. Generational conflict is a problem in many kinds of businesses that don't have what I call permanent equity. So let's imagine General Motors or Microsoft. When you buy a share of stock in General Motors or Microsoft, it lasts forever. It lasts as long as the firm does. And so even if I'm going to sell my shares in Microsoft next week, I'm still happy for Microsoft to incur costs today in order to build technology that will yield profits 10 years from now because the price at which I sell next week will reflect the buyer's expectations about what will happen 10 years from now. The share lasts indefinitely, and therefore prices paid in a market for those shares will reflect the value of the indefinite future. Well, not so in a law firm. When I retire from a law firm, whether that's Cravath or Covington and Burling, my shares simply disappear. They're extinguished. Nobody buys them back from me. They're just gone. And so if I'm a 31-year-old partner and you're a 61-year-old partner, I'm going to be a lot more interested in the future of the Because when you retire two years from now, the value of any investment you made in the firm is going to be gone.
turns.zh: 对，你看，未来是很难预知的。律所在做商业决策时，面临的不确定性和其他任何类型的企业一样。而且我得说，有很多所都走过 Weil 走过的那条路，只是它们大多数后来都改变了航向。一个好例子是 Cadwalader。Cadwalader 的全名是 Cadwalader, Wickersham & Taft。这个 Taft 就是美国前任总统兼首席大法官（chief justice），也是一位 Yale 法学院教授——我得补一句。它是一家非常非常有声望的所，一度极其赚钱。但和 Weil 一样，它没有增长。而它最终——就在最近——不得不通过与一家声望低得多的所合并来寻找归宿：Hogan Lovells。请 Cadwalader 和 Hogan 的各位见谅。但 Hogan 没有 Cadwalader 那样的历史。所以要点是：Weil 追求这个战略并不疯狂；但是，它疯狂在把这条路守得太久了一点。不过 Joe，你还问了一个更深的问题，就是：现在或者过去的合伙人，愿不愿意为未来投资？对。答案是：嗯，未必愿意。所以我最近在网上放了一个新项目，讲一个我称之为“代际冲突”（generational conflict）的概念。代际冲突是很多类型的企业都存在的一个问题，这些企业没有我所说的“永久股权”（permanent equity）。我们来想象一下 General Motors 或者 Microsoft。当你买了 General Motors 或者 Microsoft 的一股股票，它是永续存在的，和公司存在得一样久。所以，即便我下周就要卖掉我的 Microsoft 股票，我依然乐意 Microsoft 今天就发生成本、去打造能在 10 年后产生利润的技术，因为我下周卖出时的价格，会反映买家对 10 年后会发生什么的预期。股票是无限期存续的，因此市场上为这些股票支付的价格，会反映无限期未来的价值。但在律所里就不是这样了。当我从一家律所退休——不管是 Cravath 还是 Covington & Burling——我的份额就直接消失了。它们被注销了。没有人把它们从我手里买回去，它们就这么没了。所以如果我是一个 31 岁的合伙人、你是一个 61 岁的合伙人，我会对这家所的未来感兴趣得多。因为当你两年后退休时，你在这家所做过的任何投资的价值，都将化为乌有。

turns.en: This also goes back to partner incentives, right? Where if all of their compensation is based on bringing in clients and none of it is based on nurturing the next generation of talent, like no one is actually going to be paying attention to that. Like there are some great senior lawyers out there who will mentor junior associates, but they seem to be few and far between.
turns.zh: 这也回到合伙人的激励问题，对吧？如果他们所有的薪酬都基于带客户进来，而没有一点是基于培养下一代人才，那就没人会真正去关注培养人才这件事。外面确实有一些很棒的资深律师会去带初级律师，但这样凤毛麟角。

turns.en: That's right. So this problem of generational conflict, it's not just between the old and the young. It's also between the people who are here now and will also be here tomorrow and the people who are here now but might leave tomorrow. And, you know, as the pace of lateral movement has picked up, the generational conflict between present and future has become much more intense. And it feeds back into everything that happens at a firm, including compensations. If I can leave at any time, it's hard to pay me anything other than my market value. So again, turning to Wachtell and Cravath, they both had lockstep compensation periods for a long time. And under a lockstep system, lawyers get paid the same based on their seniority rather than their productivity. Well, a system like that creates winners and losers. And the losers, the people who are getting underpaid, are likely to leave. And so the pressure of lateral movement basically forces the firm into an eat-what-you-kill system. An even broader way to think about it, to return to your analogy about nations, Joe, is to say it really is like nations where people can come in and out as well. If you overtax billionaires in California, for example, they will leave. And if you pay really generous healthcare subsidies and poverty-related transfers, a lot of people who are in need of that assistance will come in. And you get the same thing in law firms, right? If you make transfers from the successful partners to the less successful ones, you'll get fewer successful partners and more unsuccessful ones.
turns.zh: 没错。所以这个代际冲突的问题，不只是老一辈和年轻人之间的冲突。它也是“现在在这儿、明天也还会在这儿的人”和“现在在这儿、但明天可能就走的人”之间的冲突。而且你知道，随着横向流动（lateral movement，指律师在所与所之间跳槽）的节奏加快，现在与未来之间的这种代际冲突变得更加剧烈。它会反馈到一家所发生的一切事情上，包括薪酬。如果我随时都能走，那除了我的市场价值之外，你很难付给我别的。所以再回到 Wachtell 和 Cravath，它们很长一段时间都采用“论资排辈”（lockstep）的薪酬体系。在 lockstep 体系下，律师按资历、而不是按产出拿一样的报酬。嗯，这样的体系会制造赢家和输家。而那些输家——那些被付少了的人——很可能会走。所以横向流动的压力，基本上把律所逼向了 eat what you kill 体系。Joe，回到你那个关于民族的类比，还有一个更宽泛的思考方式：律所其实真的很像那些人也能够进进出出的国家。比方说，如果你对加州的亿万富翁征税太重，他们就会走；而如果你提供非常慷慨的医疗补贴和与贫困相关的转移支付，很多需要这类救助的人就会涌进来。律所里发生的是同样的事，对吧？如果你从成功的合伙人那里转移支付给不那么成功的合伙人，你就会得到更少的成功合伙人、和更多的不成功合伙人。

turns.en: We've talked about this briefly on a couple of episodes in the past, but since we're talking about it again now, this whole thing of big star lateral hires, where one firm spends a lot of money to poach a ringmaker. This is a fairly new thing. In the history of big law, this is a relatively recent phenomenon.
turns.zh: 我们过去在几期节目里简短聊过这个，但既然现在又聊到了：这一整套大牌横向挖角（big star lateral hires）的事——一家所花一大笔钱去挖走一个造雨人——这在 big law 的历史上是一件相当新的事情，是一个相对晚近的现象。

turns.en: It is.
turns.zh: 确实是。

turns.en: I mean, it's really- Is this a norms thing? Was it just not the norm that this was done, and then someone broke the norm, or- Like, what is it now such that this has become a more prevalent phenomenon than.
turns.zh: 我是说，这真的是——这是一个规范（norms）的问题吗？以前只是大家不这么做，然后有人打破了这个规范，还是——现在到底是发生了什么，让它变成了一个比过去更普遍的现象？

turns.en: It used to be? It's a hard question to answer convincingly because I think ultimately it was a norms thing. There was no hard obstacle to it. There was nothing in 1975 preventing a partner from leaving Cravath and moving to Kirkland and Ellis. There's nothing preventing that. And yet they just didn't do it. They just didn't do it until really the last 20 years. And with every passing year, the volume of lateral partner movement increases. I mean, the firm that really started the action was Kirkland and Ellis. They were the first ones to do this kind of poaching at a really large scale, and they did it very well. I should say there are substantial business risks to doing that kind of poaching. When you interview a lawyer to move to your firm, you ask the lawyer how much business she has, and she's going to say, oh, I generate a gazillion dollars a year. But both professional ethics rules and that lawyer's fiduciary duties to their current firm prevent them from actually talking to their clients and asking if they'll be willing to move. Also, if the lawyer's current firm found out that they were shopping around, that lawyer might get fired. So you basically don't know. The lawyer says, I'm bringing in X amount, but you don't really know. And I think for a long time, people were just skittish about hiring under those conditions. But people have overcome their fears and they're now willing to make big bets. On the norms question, let me just say one other thing, which is that I really feel like law firms are kind of a microcosm of modernity. They really are like nations in the sense that they have one person, one vote rules. They have systems of redistribution. People relate to them in a variety of ways. They want not just money, but also satisfying social lives, a nice working space. They have multiplicitous demands of this organization they relate to. People are conflicted in how they vote to it. They're voting on their own compensation, in a sense, in the same way that we vote on our own tax rates implicitly by electing the people who will establish them. So a lot of the problems of public governance also creep into law firm governance and replicate themselves in weird ways. And so what I would say about norms is just that in the same way, all of human life has become more calculated, more self-interest seeking, more formal and more commercial, less familial, less communal, less traditional. That's happened at law firms. And so like, you know, at Cravat, there used to be, I don't know if there still is this tradition where in the partners of Cravath would be the pallbearers at a partner's future funeral. You know, like an illustrative example of like the tradition that attached to these organizations. But like that's all fading away. And when it does, people act on the basis of self-interest seeking and money. There's nothing wrong with that. It's just a very modern way of thinking about human relations.
turns.zh: 以前是这样吗？这个问题很难给出一个令人信服的答案，因为我觉得归根结底它是一个规范的问题。做这件事并没有什么硬性障碍。1975 年没有任何东西阻止一个合伙人离开 Cravath、跳到 Kirkland & Ellis，没有东西阻止这么做。可他们就是不做。他们就是不做——直到最近这 20 年才这样。而且每过一年，合伙人横向流动的规模都在增加。我是说，真正把这波动作带起来的所是 Kirkland & Ellis。他们是第一批大规模搞这种挖角的，而且做得非常漂亮。我得说，搞这种挖角是有相当大的商业风险的。当你面试一个想跳槽到你所的律师时，你会问她手上有多少业务，她会说“哦，我一年能创收天文数字的钱”。但无论是职业伦理规则、还是那个律师对现东家负有的信义义务（fiduciary duties），都不允许她真的去跟她的客户谈、问他们愿不愿意跟着跳。而且，如果那个律师现在的所发现她在外面找下家，她可能被开除。所以你基本上无从知晓。律师说她能带来 X 数量的业务，但你其实并不真的知道。我觉得很长一段时间里，大家就是不敢在这种条件下招人。但人们已经克服了恐惧，现在愿意下大注了。关于规范这个问题，我还要再说一点：我真的觉得律所某种程度是现代性的一个缩影（microcosm of modernity）。它们真的很像国家——它们有“一人一票”的规则，有再分配的体系。人们以各种方式和它们打交道，想要的不只是钱，还有令人满意的社交生活、一个不错的工作空间；他们对这个自己身处其中的组织有着五花八门的诉求。人们在怎么给它投票这件事上是矛盾的。他们其实是在给自己的薪酬投票，某种意义上，就像我们通过选举那些将要设定税率的人、从而潜移默化地给自己的税率投票一样。所以很多公共治理的问题，也会悄悄爬进律所的治理里，并以奇怪的方式重演。关于规范，我要说的就是：正如全部的人类生活都变得更算计、更追逐私利、更正式、更商业化，更少了家庭味、更少了共同体味、更少了传统味——这在律所里也发生了。所以，你知道，在 Cravath，过去有一个传统——我不知道现在还有没有——就是 Cravath 的合伙人们会去给一位合伙人的葬礼当抬棺人（pallbearers）。你知道，这是一个能说明附着在这些组织上的那种传统的、很有代表性的例子。但这一切都在消退。而当它消退时，人们就会基于追逐私利和金钱来行动。这没什么错。这只是一种非常现代的思考人际关系的方式。

turns.en: Joe doesn't like the term peak capitalism, but it's very peak capitalism.
turns.zh: Joe 不喜欢“巅峰资本主义”（peak capitalism）这个说法，但这确实非常“巅峰资本主义”。

turns.en: Come on. The peak could get higher still.
turns.zh: 得了吧。这个“巅峰”还能再高呢。

turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.en: It's true. It's true. I just want to go back to the sort of classic theory of ownership stuff. And I mentioned in the beginning, we do have some investor owned law firms. And there's a famous example that you talk about in your paper, an investor owned law firm that came very, very close to collapse. But because they didn't have the partnership model, they ended up being able to restructure and sort of emerge from the bankruptcy process more or less in one piece. Can you talk about how that difference in ownership structure actually played in that example?
turns.zh: 是真的，是真的。我就想回到那套经典的所有权理论上。我开头提到过，我们确实有一些投资人持有的律所。你论文里讲到一个著名的例子：一家投资人持有的律所，一度非常非常接近倒闭。但正因为他们不是合伙制，他们最后得以重组，基本上算是完整地走出了破产程序。你能讲讲，在那个例子里，所有权结构的这个差异实际上是怎么发挥作用的吗？

turns.en: Yeah. So the firm was called Slater & Gordon. It was a conventional partner-owned law firm in Australia that went public and listed on a stock exchange when Australia changed its rules about lawyer ownership back in the 90s. And after going public in Australia, it used the capital it raised to acquire other firms in both Australia and the UK, and it eventually listed in the UK as well. So it was basically just an investor-owned business. And it had so much capital and so much ability to raise it that it eventually did kind of add-on acquisitions of related businesses that weren't law firms and acquired a business called, if I remember correctly, Quindel, which was... a medical services firm as well as a legal services firm for people who'd been in car accidents. The idea was somebody gets in a car accident, we'll represent you as a lawyer and treat your whiplash. Well, Quindel, it turned out, was just a fraud. The accounting, the books had been cooked.
turns.zh: 对。那家所叫 Slater & Gordon。它本来是澳大利亚一家传统的合伙人持有的律所，后来在澳大利亚 90 年代修改了关于律师所有权的规则之后，它上市了、在证券交易所挂牌。在澳大利亚上市之后，它用募来的资本去收购了澳大利亚和英国的其他律所，最终也在英国上了市。所以它基本上就是一家投资人持有的企业。它有那么多资本、那么强的融资能力，以至于它最后确实做了一些对相关业务——那些不是律所的业务——的“补充收购”（add-on acquisitions），收购了一家我记得叫 Quindell 的公司，那是一家医疗服务公司，同时也是一家为出过车祸的人提供法律服务的公司。这个想法是：某人出了车祸，我们作为律师代理你，同时给你治疗挥鞭伤（whiplash）。结果呢，Quindell 其实就是一场骗局。它的会计、它的账本是被做过的。

turns.en: I'm shocked.
turns.zh: 我很震惊。

turns.en: I'm shocked. So Slater and Gordon realizes that it's massively overpaid for this asset that now turns out to be worth a fraction of its accounting value. So it was just insolvent in the same way An auto parts manufacturer would be insolvent if it made a bad acquisition. All right. So what happened was the firm went to the hedge funds that had lent it money. It went to the banks that lent it money and said, we got to do a workout. They wiped away the equity. They turned the junior debt into equity. They split the business between its Australian and UK pieces, and they kept operating. And the question is, and they're both still in business today. Why didn't that collapse in the way the Weill Gottschall collapsed? Well, the answer is because the lawyers weren't owners of the firm. Their pay did not decline when the business became less profitable. They didn't face any risk of liability. They were like the pilots at Delta Airlines or the factory workers at General Motors, both of whom continued working for those businesses when they went bankrupt because they continued to get paid. The key difference in an investor-owned firm is that investors can't pull back their money Right. In an investor owned firm, you can sell your shares, but you can't take back the chunk of the company's assets that correspond to your interest. So Slater and Gordon was able to say to its equity holders, you're wiped out, go away. And they just did. But the money stayed inside the firm. Now, imagine if Weill Gottschall tried that. Imagine if it said to the equity holders, you're wiped out. The creditors of the firm now own the firm. What would those equity holders do? They would go to Cravath because they're partners of the firm. They could just walk away.
turns.zh: 我也很震惊。于是 Slater & Gordon 意识到，它为一项资产付出了过高的代价，而这项资产如今被证明只值其账面价值的一小部分。所以它就资不抵债了，就像一家汽车零部件制造商做了一笔糟糕的收购之后会资不抵债一样。好。那么发生的情况是：这家所去找了借钱给它的对冲基金，去找了借钱给它的银行，说：“我们得做一次债务重组（workout）。”他们把股权清零了，把次级债务（junior debt）转成了股权，把业务拆分成了澳大利亚和英国两块，然后继续经营。而问题是——他们两块业务今天都还在经营——为什么它没有像 Weil Gotshal 那样垮掉？答案是：因为律师们不是这家所的所有者。当业务变得不那么赚钱时，他们的薪酬并没有下降，他们也没有面临任何责任风险。他们就像 Delta 航空的飞行员、或者 General Motors 的车间工人一样——这两家企业破产时，飞行员和工人都在继续为它们工作，因为他们能继续拿到报酬。投资人持有的企业里，关键的区别在于：投资人没法把自己的钱抽回去。对。在一家投资人持有的企业里，你可以卖掉你的股份，但你没法把公司资产中对应你那份额的那一块拿走。所以 Slater & Gordon 能够对它那些股权持有人说：“你们被清零了，走开吧。”而他们就真的走开了。但钱留在了公司内部。现在，想象一下如果 Weil Gotshal 也来这一招。想象一下如果它对股权持有人说：“你们被清零了，这家所现在归债权人所有。”那些股权持有人会怎么做？他们会跑去 Cravath，因为他们是这家所的合伙人，他们可以直接走人。

turns.en: So what happened? So actually, just for including me, like in the last several weeks, so the company collapses. Is there something called while still? What is the wind down look like? Is there a last lawyer who leaves like someone who has to turn? You know, someone's got to be the last lawyer to like find a job somewhere else. How does it actually, what's the actual good night process?
turns.zh: 那后来怎么样了？其实就在最近这几周——算是让我也搞明白点——这家公司就垮了。有没有一个叫“while still”的东西？清盘（wind down）看起来是什么样的？会不会有最后一个离开的律师——就像得有人去关灯锁门那种。你知道，总得有人是最后一个、还得去别处找份工作的律师。它实际上是怎么……这个“道晚安”（good night）的流程到底是怎么回事？

turns.en: It's going to be fascinating to watch this all unfold. So let me first of all say, I think that not surprisingly for a firm that does bankruptcy for a living, Wiles actually handled the wind down remarkably well. The best decision they made was to wind the thing down quickly. Remember fraudulent transfer liabilities. Fraudulent transfer liability commences the moment the firm becomes insolvent, and it ends the moment the firm winds up. And it's really hard to say when a law firm becomes insolvent, not least because they have very few debts. But in many other collapsed firms, that period has lasted six months, eight months. At Dewey and LaBeouf, it was something like eight or nine months. And so by calling an end quickly, Weil basically avoided a bunch of fraudulent transfer liability for its partners. So what they're doing now is winding up the firm. There's a few lawyers still left at the firm. They need a place to continue representing their clients. Their clients have ongoing needs that need to be serviced. And to the extent people still at Weil are continuing to represent clients, the fees for those representations are all going to go into Weil. But all of the cash, including the fees that are brought in over the next few months, all of that's going to get eaten up by creditors. Now, Weill didn't have a lot of financial debts. That is to say, they didn't have bank borrowings. But it still has lots of creditors who have claims on the firm. The biggest category by far is going to be the landlords. Now, people often say, well, you know, landlords, rent doesn't account for that big of a chunk of law firm's revenues. That's true month to month. But if there's 10 years outstanding on that lease on the General Motors building on Fifth Avenue and 59th Street, the landlord can probably make a claim for all 10 years of it today. Well, that's going to be more than enough to eat up whatever cash is left inside that firm. So even though the partners at Weill are not going to face a bunch of liability, things are not going to be happy for them. Law firm partner compensation is ordinarily spread out unevenly across the year. Every month or every quarter, they'll get paid a little bit of money. But then they'll get a big chunk amounting to like 50 or 60 percent of their total annual compensation around mid-January when the books for the prior year have been settled. What this means in effect is that the partners at Weill Godshall worked for 10 months out of the year and they're never going to see the 50 percent of their compensation for that period that would have been paid to them in January. That's all going to get eaten up by creditors. So Kind of sad for the partners at Weill Godshaw.
turns.zh: 看着这一切一步步展开会非常有意思。首先我得说，我觉得——对一家靠做破产为生的所来说，这一点也不意外——Weil 实际上把这次清盘处理得相当好。他们做的最明智的决定，就是快速地把这件事了结掉。记得那个“欺诈性转让责任”吗？欺诈性转让责任从这家所变得资不抵债的那一刻开始，到它清盘结束的那一刻终止。而要说清楚一家律所什么时候变得资不抵债，其实非常难，尤其因为它们几乎没有债务。但在其他很多垮掉的所里，这段时间持续了 6 个月、8 个月。在 Dewey & LeBoeuf，大概是 8 到 9 个月。所以通过尽快宣布结束，Weil 基本上帮它的合伙人避免了一大堆欺诈性转让责任。所以他们现在在做的，就是清算这家所。所里还剩下几个律师，他们需要一个地方来继续代理他们的客户；他们的客户有持续的需求需要被服务。而对于仍然留在 Weil、继续代理客户的人来说，这些代理业务产生的费用都会进 Weil。但所有的现金——包括接下来几个月带进来的费用——都会被债权人吃光。好，Weil 并没有很多金融债务，也就是说他们没有银行借款。但它仍然有很多对这家所拥有债权的债权人。最大的一类，毫无疑问，将是房东。人们常说：“你知道，房东、租金占律所营收的比例没那么大。”按月看，这是对的。但如果第五大道和 59 街那栋 General Motors 大楼的租约还有 10 年到期，房东今天大概可以就这 10 年全部主张债权。嗯，这将绰绰有余地把这家所里剩下的任何现金都吃光。所以，即便 Weil 的合伙人不会面临一大堆责任，他们的日子也不会好过。律所合伙人的薪酬通常在一年里分布得很不均匀。每个月或者每个季度，他们会拿到一点点钱；但然后他们会拿到一大块，相当于全年总薪酬的 50% 到 60%，大约在 1 月中旬——上一年度的账结算完的时候。这实际意味着，Weil Gotshal 的合伙人在这一年里干了 10 个月的活，而他们永远也拿不到本该在 1 月付给他们的那 50% 的薪酬了，那部分会全被债权人吃光。所以对 Weil Gotshal 的合伙人来说，有点惨。

turns.en: Yeah, it's a rough year.
turns.zh: 是啊，这是难熬的一年。

turns.en: I genuinely feel bad for them. A big question is whether the firm's going to file for bankruptcy. They've said they don't intend to, and I think they probably won't have to. The reason is that bankruptcy is fundamentally a solution to a collective action problem. You have a lot of creditors who need to work together to recover on the debts, and you need one person who can represent them. The collective action problem at Weill Gottschall is not going to be as acute as it was at many other law firms, such as Dewey and LaBeouf, for example. Because first off, there aren't going to be many creditors. There'll be a few landlords, basically. And there aren't going to be that many debts for it to collect upon because the partners aren't likely to be liable. Like in Dewey, you needed a bankruptcy to trustee to go out and sue each one of the partners. And famously, there were a few partners at Dewey who declared personal bankruptcy as a result of those liabilities. But we don't need anyone to do that process of collection at Wild Gottschalk because the partners aren't going to be liable.
turns.zh: 我是真的挺替他们难过的。一个大问题是：这家所会不会申请破产。他们已经说了不打算申请，而且我觉得他们大概也不必申请。原因是：破产从根本上说，是对一个集体行动问题（collective action problem）的解决方案。你有一大堆债权人，他们需要协同起来去收回债务，而你需要一个能代表他们的人。Weil Gotshal 的集体行动问题，不会像很多其他律所——比如 Dewey & LeBoeuf——那样尖锐。因为首先，债权人不会有很多，基本上就几个房东；而且不会有那么多可供收回的债务，因为合伙人不太可能承担责任。像在 Dewey 那样，你需要一个破产受托人（trustee）出去、把每一个合伙人都告一遍；而且众所周知，Dewey 有几个合伙人因为这些责任而申请了个人破产。但在 Weil Gotshal，我们不需要任何人去做那个追讨的过程，因为合伙人不会承担责任。

turns.en: Yeah, we're recording this on November 10th. And there's a new story just across the Bloomberg now saying that the Weil partners have voted to dissolve the firm and they've named their wind down committee. So I guess they'll be making some decisions soon. But I hadn't realized this, but like the ultimate injury added to insult the woman who was going to lead the firm as executive partner, Ramona Nee. I didn't realize she's been hired by Kirkland Ellis. Yeah. So she said she didn't want to take on the executive partnership and things kind of spiraled from there.
turns.zh: 对，我们是在 11 月 10 日录的这期。就在现在，Bloomberg 上又出了一条新报道，说 Weil 的合伙人已经投票决定解散这家所，并且任命了他们的清算委员会（wind down committee）。所以我想他们很快会做一些决定。但我之前没意识到——不过这真是伤口上撒盐——那位本来要作为执行合伙人（executive partner）执掌这家所的女性，Ramona Nee，我原来不知道她被 Kirkland & Ellis 挖走了。对。所以她说她不想接下执行合伙人这个位子，然后事情就从那儿开始急转直下。

turns.en: You know, I have to say the moment that I thought, wow, the end is near for Weill Gottschall, I knew that they were in trouble for since midsummer, basically. But the moment when I thought it's inevitable, it was when I found out that Ramona Nee was not going to be the chair of the firm and that there was a debate about whether she had known that for several months before disclosing it to the rest of the partners. You know, A law firm collapse is kind of like a bank run. It's a crisis of confidence. Franklin Delano Roosevelt said, we have nothing to fear but fear itself. And what he meant was the fear that propels bank runs is itself a thing to fear. And I think a big part of Weill's problems, which I didn't describe earlier, is that in addition to having unfavorable economics, it had by all accounts a pretty toxic governance culture. And when Ramona Nee, when that news about her came out, I thought, whatever faith was left in the management of this firm is going to be gone. And people are not going to have any reason to stay other than money.
turns.zh: 你知道，我得说，让我心想“哇，Weil Gotshal 的大限到了”的那一刻——其实基本上从仲夏起我就知道他们有麻烦了——但让我觉得“这是不可避免的了”的那一刻，是我得知 Ramona Nee 不会出任这家所的主席、而且关于她是否在向其他合伙人披露之前好几个月就已经知道这件事、还存在一场争论的时候。你知道，一家律所的倒闭，某种程度就像一场银行挤兑，它是一场信心危机。Franklin Delano Roosevelt 说过：“我们唯一需要恐惧的，就是恐惧本身。”他的意思是，那种引发银行挤兑的恐惧，本身就是一件值得恐惧的东西。而我觉得 Weil 问题的一大块——这一点我前面没讲——就是：除了经济面不利之外，据各方说法，它还有一种相当有毒（toxic）的治理文化。而当 Ramona Nee、当关于她的那个消息曝出来时，我想，人们对这家所管理层残存的那点信任，就要荡然无存了。而人们除了钱之外，不会再有任何理由留下来。

turns.en: Well, can you talk a little bit more about that? Because when I think about law firms, again, much like banks, all of these companies or partnerships, they like to talk about the importance of culture and putting the client first and we're all one big family. But then when you look at what's been going on recently with some of these lateral hires, with the way some partners treat junior associates and stuff like that, is there culture left at a lot of these firms?
turns.zh: 那你能不能再多讲讲这个？因为当我想到律所时——再一次，很像银行——所有这些公司或者合伙制企业，都喜欢谈论文化有多重要、要把客户放在第一位、我们都是一家人。可是当你看看最近这些横向挖角、看看某些合伙人怎么对待初级律师之类的，这些所里还剩下什么文化吗？

turns.en: Less and less, less and less. I mean, again, law firms are microcosms of modernity, right? There's a loneliness crisis for a reason. We all love to talk about how much we value our families, and yet we so often move away from them. We have fewer children. We have less close relationships with our siblings and our parents. And yeah, I think law firms are finding it harder and harder and harder to sustain. The way I think about it is that families are places of what my Yale University sociology colleague, Nick Christakis calls mild hierarchy. He describes mild hierarchy as the default mode of organization in every small to medium-sized group of human beings. Well, that's what feels like a family. Like dad and mom are sort of in charge, but like, you know, eventually the kids will take care of them and they sort of have obligations to the kids. Law firms could feel like that in the days of lockstep compensation. But like now that you can fire brother, And now that sister can leave, it feels less like a family. Or maybe in some weird way, it feels more like a family now that there's all these news stories about children cutting off their parents, right?
turns.zh: 越来越少，越来越少。我是说，再一次，律所是现代性的缩影，对吧？会有“孤独危机”（loneliness crisis）是有原因的。我们都爱说我们有多看重家庭，可我们又常常离家庭远远的；我们生更少的孩子；我们和兄弟姐妹、和父母的关系也没那么亲密了。而且，是的，我觉得律所越来越、越来越、越来越难维系那种感觉。我是这么想的：家庭是那种我 Yale 大学社会学同事 Nick Christakis 所称的“温和等级”（mild hierarchy）的地方。他把温和等级描述为每一个中小型人类群体的默认组织方式。嗯，那就是“家”的感觉。就像爸爸和妈妈算是当家的，但你知道，孩子们最终会照顾他们，而他们对孩子们也多少负有一些义务。在 lockstep 薪酬的年代，律所可以给人一种那样的感觉。但现在你可以“开除兄弟”了，现在“姐妹”可以走人了，它就没那么像个家了。或者，也许以一种奇怪的方式，它现在更像个家了——毕竟现在到处都是子女和父母断绝关系的新闻，对吧？

turns.en: It's a dysfunctional family.
turns.zh: 这是一个功能失调的家庭。

turns.en: It's a modern family is what it is, which is a very disconnected one.
turns.zh: 它就是一个现代家庭，就是这么回事——一个非常彼此疏离的家庭。

turns.en: This is a very deep conversation. As you mentioned, and I've heard about, and maybe we'll do an episode at some point about some of these like AI native law firms. And I know there are some efforts- Like you mentioned Arizona, where there may be like an investor bag. People are trying different models and so forth. And actually, speaking of Kirk O'Neillis and AI, there was a story earlier this year, like they're going to build their own AI model, et cetera, and have their own fine-tuned model and house. I'm just curious from your perspective, from this sort of the generational warfare framework that you characterize AI, et cetera, like can you give us some thoughts on like whether you think that for some of these big legacy firms, they're going to successfully, A, make investments that will just like sort of kind of come out of the senior partner's pocket in a way they might never, they might not be around long enough to see the fruits and actually like sort of like navigate a transition to some meaningfully different type of economics.
turns.zh: 这是一场非常有深度的对话。就像你提到的，我也听说过——也许我们哪一期会做一做这些“AI 原生”（AI native）律所的话题。我知道有一些尝试——就像你提到的 Arizona，那里也许可以有投资人入股。人们在尝试各种各样的模式。而且其实说到 Kirkland & Ellis 和 AI，今年早些时候有一条报道，说他们要打造自己的 AI 模型等等，要有自己的、内部微调（fine-tuned）的模型。我就很好奇，从你的视角、从你所描述的那种代际战争（generational warfare）的框架来看 AI 等等，你能不能给我们讲讲：你觉得对一些大型的、传统的老所而言，它们能不能成功地——第一，做出那种投资（而这种投资基本上就是从资深合伙人兜里掏钱，而他们可能都撑不到看见成果的那一天）——并且真正地驾驭一场转型，走向某种有意义的、不同类型的经济学。

turns.en: And so if you believe my story about general conflict, you would predict as I do that, Although AI will transform the practice of law, very little AI technology will be developed by law firms because it's really hard for the partners of today to incur a big expense for the benefit of the partners of five years from now because the partners of today and the partners of five years from now will be different. People will enter, people will exit. Okay, but that doesn't mean that law firms never invest at all. They invest in branding. They invest in the training of associates. They invest in the renovation of office space. They've always made investments, just not really big ones. And I predict that's how investment in AI will unfold. They will make investments, just not really big ones. A nice illustration is law firms renovate office space. They don't buy office space. Law firms will renovate AI. They won't buy or develop AI. They will rent it. They'll pay licensing fees to third-party providers. Now, Let's talk about Kirkland and Latham, both of which have announced large investments in AI technology. Why are they able to do this? First off, the investments aren't that big in the scheme of those firms' revenues. I'm shooting from the hip here a little bit, but it's no accident that those two firms are the largest law firms by revenue in the world because they're the ones that can handle a big investment. So Kirkland's revenues are something like $ 10 billion a year. And they've announced that they're going to make a $ 500 million investment over a period of five years. Well, if we assume Kirkland continues the same growth trajectory of revenue growth that it's been on, over those five years, it'll probably earn something like $ 80 million. Well, $ 500 million in the context of $ 80 billion is not that. much. Like the partners might just shrug and say, yeah, okay, fine. You're taking 1% of my compensation to benefit the partners at five years from now. That's okay. Especially because a lot of those partners will be partners five years from now. The other thing is they're pacing it over five years so that they can align the incurring of an expense with the earning of the revenue, right? As they develop this technology, it will bring in more revenue and they will pace the development of the technology to coincide with the earning of the revenue. The other thing I would say about it is, and apologies to the Kirkland and Ellis people listening to this podcast, they say it's going to be $ 500 million. Who's keeping track? Like, what is the AI investment? I don't really know. they have an incentive to expansively characterize a lot of what they do as an AI investment. So the bottom line is it's a relatively modest investment spread out over a long period of time that will coincide with the earning of revenues.
turns.zh: 所以，如果你相信我关于代际冲突的说法，你就会像我一样预测：尽管 AI 会改变法律执业，但很少有 AI 技术会由律所自己开发出来。因为对今天的合伙人来说，为了 5 年后那些合伙人的利益而去承担一大笔开支，真的很难——因为今天的合伙人和 5 年后的合伙人将是不同的人，会有人进来、有人出去。好，但这并不意味着律所从不投资。他们投资品牌，投资对初级律师的培训，投资办公空间的翻新。他们一直都在做投资，只是不做大额投资。而我预测，AI 上的投资就会这么展开：他们会做投资，只是不做大额的。一个很好的例子是：律所翻新办公空间，但他们不购买办公空间。律所会“翻新”AI，但不会购买或开发 AI；他们会租用它，会向第三方提供商付授权费（licensing fees）。好，我们来聊聊 Kirkland 和 Latham，这两家都宣布了在 AI 技术上的大额投资。他们为什么能做到这一点？首先，这些投资相对于这两家所的营收规模来说，并不算大。我这里有点凭感觉估计，但那两家所恰恰是全球按营收算最大的律所，这不是巧合——因为他们才是能扛得住大额投资的人。Kirkland 的营收大概是每年 100 亿美元（$10 billion）。他们宣布要在 5 年里投资 5 亿美元（$500 million）。那么，如果我们假设 Kirkland 在这 5 年里延续它一直以来的营收增长轨迹，它大概会赚到 8000 万美元（$80 million）左右。嗯，800 亿美元（$80 billion）背景下的 5 亿美元，就不算太多了。合伙人们也许就会耸耸肩说：“行吧，好，可以。你拿走我薪酬的 1%，去造福 5 年后的合伙人，这没问题。”尤其是因为其中很多合伙人 5 年后还会是合伙人。另一点是，他们把它分摊到 5 年里，这样就能让开支的发生和营收的赚取对齐，对吧？随着他们开发这项技术，它会带来更多营收，而他们会把技术开发的节奏和营收的赚取节奏对上。关于这件事我要说的另一点是——请 Kirkland & Ellis 那些在听这档播客的人见谅——他们说这会是 5 亿美元。谁在盯着这个数呢？比如说，什么才算 AI 投资？我其实并不真的清楚。他们有动机把自己做的很多事情都宽泛地表述成 AI 投资。所以底线是：这是一笔相对适度的投资，分摊在一段很长的时间里，而且会和营收的赚取对齐。

turns.en: Yeah, it's not like their outside shareholders are going to call them up on it and be like, you said $ 500 million. turns.en: Let's ask why people should care. Okay, I think there's a few reasons. One is it has happened to many other firms. We haven't talked about this, but This has happened to dozens of firms. In my paper, I studied three dozen firms. In the years since I published the paper, there's been more. Bingham, McCutcheon, Strzok and Strzok and Levin. There will be more. I promise you there will be more. The other is that what's happening at law firms is diagnostic of what's happening in the legal industry generally. It's tremendous pressure on profitability such that if you don't keep up, you're in the doghouse. Huge amounts of lateral partner movement. Also, law firms as microcosms of modernity. I also think that what happens in law firms is consistent with what happens in other kinds of what I call impermanent equity businesses. So there's lots of businesses where equity interests don't last forever. Mutual funds and hedge funds, when you redeem, your interest terminates. Mutual insurance companies, which are sort of owned by their policyholders, if you stop renewing your policy, you're no longer an equity holder. They experience some of the same problems as law firms. Hedge funds, for example, are famously vulnerable to runs. just like Wild God Shaw. So I study organizations broadly. I write about investment funds, about law firms, about marriage even. And I find law firms an interesting laboratory in which to study themes in organization. Maybe here's the biggest one of all. The central ideological struggle of the Cold War between the United States and Soviet Union was whether the means of production would be owned by investors, that is to say capitalists, or by workers. And what law firms illustrate is some of the perils and promise of worker ownership. It's the path not taken by industry more generally.
turns.zh: 那我们来问问人们为什么应该关心。好，我觉得有几个原因。一个是，这种事已经发生在很多其他所身上了。这个我们还没聊到，但已经有几十家所发生过这种事了。在我的论文里，我研究了三打（three dozen，即 36 家）律所。而在我发表论文之后的这些年里，又出现了更多：Bingham McCutchen、Strzok & Levin。还会有更多的。我向你保证，还会有更多。另一个原因是，律所里正在发生的事，是整个律师行业正在发生的事的一个诊断信号（diagnostic）。盈利上承受着巨大的压力，以至于如果你跟不上，你就麻烦了；还有大量的合伙人横向流动；而且，律所作为现代性的缩影。我还觉得，律所里发生的事，和其他我所谓的“非永久股权”（impermanent equity）企业里发生的事是一致的。有很多企业，其股权权益并不是永续的。共同基金（mutual funds）和对冲基金，当你赎回时，你的权益就终止了。相互保险公司（mutual insurance companies），它们某种程度上是由保单持有人拥有的，如果你不再续保，你就不再是股权持有人了。它们经历着和律所一样的一些问题。比如说，对冲基金就以容易被挤兑而著称，就跟 Weil Gotshal 一样。所以我广泛地研究各种组织。我写投资基金、写律所、甚至写婚姻。而我觉得律所是一个有意思的实验室，可以在其中研究组织的一些主题。也许这里是所有主题里最大的一个：美国和苏联之间冷战的核心意识形态之争，就是生产资料（means of production）究竟该由投资人——也就是资本家——持有，还是由工人持有。而律所示给我们的，是工人所有制（worker ownership）的一些危险与前景。它是整个行业普遍没有走的那条路。
